title: Follow me (Mark 1:14–20)
hook: Mark's favorite word: immediately they left their nets

segments.voice: Yesterday: the heavens torn open, a voice saying beloved, and then the desert. Your line was beloved, then the desert. Did the first word go with you? Day one hundred fifty-nine.

Early morning on the Sea of Galilee. It's really a lake, about thirteen miles long, and the fishing is hard work: nets, boats, cold water, a family business. Two brothers, Simon and Andrew, are standing in the shallows casting a net. A man walks along the shore. He stops, looks at them, and says two words, more or less: follow me. And then Mark tells us what they did, and the word he uses is the heartbeat of his whole gospel. Down the beach, it happens again, with two more brothers, James and John, mending nets in their father's boat. You've probably done the opposite a thousand times: meant to, planned to, will get to it. Today's word is Mark's favorite.
screen: `EARLY MORNING ON THE LAKE.` → `TWO BROTHERS CASTING A NET.` → `FOLLOW ME.`

segments.voice: Immediately. In Greek, euthys. Mark uses it about forty times in sixteen short chapters, more than all the other gospels put together. The King James Bible often translates it straightway. Once you notice it, you can't stop: straightway he saw the heavens torn, immediately the Spirit drove him out, and now this. First, Mark sets the scene. John the Baptist has been arrested. Jesus comes into Galilee announcing: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel." Repent there means turn around, change direction. And then the lake. He sees Simon and Andrew casting a net, and says: "Come ye after me, and I will make you to become fishers of men." A fisherman's joke, almost: you catch fish now, you'll catch people. And then: "And straightway they forsook their nets, and followed him." Straightway. Immediately. No negotiation, no three-month notice. A little further on, James and John are in their boat with their father, Zebedee. Jesus calls them, and they leave their father in the boat with the hired men, and go. Mark doesn't tell us what they were thinking. He doesn't say whether they'd met Jesus before; John's gospel suggests some of them had. He just shows the speed. Readers have always noticed the cost, too: a father left sitting in a boat. For Mark, immediately is not recklessness. It's the rhythm of a story where God's time has arrived and can't wait. Christians hear it as a question put to them: what's the net in my hands, and what would it mean to put it down?
screen: `EUTHYS — ABOUT FORTY TIMES.` · `THE TIME IS FULFILLED.` · `FISHERS OF MEN.` · `A FATHER LEFT IN THE BOAT.` · then, large: `STRAIGHTWAY THEY FORSOOK THEIR NETS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of one good thing you've been putting off. Not a huge life change. Something small and kind or true. Texting a friend who's struggling. Apologizing. Signing up to help. Returning the call. Opening the Bible you meant to open. Notice the net in your hands: the reasons, the timing, the someday. For these two minutes, just picture putting it down and doing the thing. If you pray, you can ask for the nerve to do it today. The bell holds the time.
Immediately. In Greek, euthys. Mark's favorite word, about forty times, the heartbeat of a story that won't wait.
Your line: leave the nets. Today, do one good thing immediately, the moment you think of it. Day one hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Christians read the calling of the first disciples as a call to their own lives, and churches often read it when commissioning people for new work or ministry.

original.note: Greek: immediately, straightway — Mark's favorite word.

trapdoor: what you thought: immediately just means quickly.
what it means: Mark's heartbeat word. God's time has come, and the story moves before anyone can stall.
what a scholar hears: euthys, about 40 times in Mark against a handful elsewhere; often a narrative connective, 'and then', as much as literal speed.

notes: Frequency of euthys in Mark: commonly given as 41 or 42 (depending on text); 'about forty' used. 'More than all the other gospels put together': Matthew ~18, Luke ~7, John ~3 (with variation). Confirm.
Sea of Galilee about 13 miles (21 km) long: confirm.
John 1:35–42 suggests Andrew and Simon had met Jesus earlier: stated as 'suggests'. Confirm.
'Repent' glossed as 'turn around, change direction' (metanoia, change of mind): confirm phrasing.
Care: 'fishers of men' kept as the KJV quotation; the voice glosses it as 'catch people'.
